extraction.note: Lossless analytical baseline extracted before applying refreshed research. Existing visual phase values are preserved separately from epistemic status.

boundary.purpose: Baseline inquiry encoded by the existing four-view Team Zig systems map.

nodes.label: Member-only
nodes.subtitle: Program relationship
nodes.definition: A person who belongs to the loyalty program but does not currently hold a banking relationship with the client.
nodes.roleInSystem: This population sustains the open program ecosystem through earning, redemption and partner participation. It is also the largest immediate population from which relevant banking relationships might be created.
nodes.whyItMatters: The program was designed to serve people beyond the bank. Preserving credible standalone value is therefore necessary both for member trust and for the client’s future relationship opportunity.
nodes.known: Member-only participants can receive program and partner value without becoming clients. Research shows that members judge programs by usable value, flexibility and reliable delivery—not ownership alone.
nodes.provisional: The active size of this population, the data that may be used for banking decisioning, and the proportion with a relevant banking need remain unconfirmed.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Use permissioned member context to recognize genuine financial needs and present bank-connected value without making conversion a condition for receiving worthwhile program value.

nodes.label: Member-client
nodes.subtitle: Program + banking relationship
nodes.definition: A person who simultaneously participates in the loyalty program and holds a banking relationship with the client.
nodes.roleInSystem: This is the strategic intersection where program value, banking value and partner value can potentially be coordinated across one relationship.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client expects the intersection to support deeper engagement and greater relationship value. Bank-linked products already demonstrate that members can receive additional earning routes and benefits.
nodes.known: Member-clients may have access to a higher potential value ceiling through connected products, enhanced earning and integrated channels.
nodes.provisional: Holding both relationships does not prove engagement, affinity or incremental value. The combined value must still be relevant, used, fulfilled and realized.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Coordinate program, banking and partner value so the intersection produces recognizably better outcomes rather than simply a larger number of linked accounts.

nodes.label: Client-only
nodes.subtitle: Banking relationship
nodes.definition: A banking client who does not currently participate in this loyalty program.
nodes.roleInSystem: This population can enter the intersection through relevant program enrolment. Existing transactions and participation in other reward products may indicate potential fit.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client already has channels, products and permissioned banking context that may help explain where program participation could add value.
nodes.known: A client may already use cashback, points or co-branded products outside this program. Those behaviours show broader loyalty engagement, but not engagement with this specific program.
nodes.provisional: Transaction activity is only a relevance signal. It does not prove interest, consent, product suitability or willingness to manage another loyalty relationship.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Identify where program participation complements an existing client need, then reduce the friction required to enrol, earn and realize the first meaningful benefit.

nodes.label: Partner ecosystem
nodes.subtitle: Merchants • experiences • business relationships
nodes.definition: Merchants and business partners that contribute products, services, offers, access or experiences to the loyalty ecosystem.
nodes.roleInSystem: Partners expand what members can earn, access and redeem while connecting the program to everyday and aspirational needs.
nodes.whyItMatters: Partner quality, frequency and relevance determine practical value more than the nominal number of brands in the ecosystem.
nodes.known: Partners can receive sales, attention, repeat purchasing and potential share-of-wallet gains. They may also receive permissioned or aggregated performance insight.
nodes.provisional: The incrementality of partner sales, actual data-sharing arrangements, offer funding and partner economics are not yet established.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Create a reciprocal value exchange in which relevant partner contributions strengthen engagement and demonstrated partner returns encourage continued participation.

nodes.label: Member value
nodes.subtitle: Potential → accessible → realized
nodes.definition: The financial, functional, experiential and emotional value that a person can potentially access through the program and its ecosystem.
nodes.roleInSystem: Member value is the exchange that gives people a reason to participate. Points are an intermediate mechanism—not the final outcome.
nodes.whyItMatters: Both interviews show that members translate points into tangible savings or experiences while also valuing flexibility, access, recognition, convenience and dependable service.
nodes.known: Value can exist before it is realized. Awareness, eligibility, accessibility, fulfilment and redemption determine whether potential value becomes useful.
nodes.provisional: The relative importance of each value type differs by member and context. More available benefits can also increase complexity and management effort.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Make value easier to understand, access, use and validate while preserving enough flexibility for different member needs.

nodes.label: Meaningful engagement
nodes.subtitle: Frequency • breadth • continuity • completion • progression
nodes.definition: A sustained pattern of participation through which members, clients and partners repeatedly access, contribute to or realize relevant value.
nodes.roleInSystem: Engagement is the primary behaviour this system must explain. It applies across all three populations and precedes potential relationship deepening or movement into the member-client intersection.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client uses engagement as a strategic objective. We distinguished it from activation and participation so the map does not mistake isolated activity for a durable relationship.
nodes.known: Participation is observable through actions such as earning, redeeming, using benefits or adopting relevant products. Activation initiates or renews that participation; repeated participation develops into engagement.
nodes.provisional: Engagement does not automatically cause conversion, affinity or revenue. Its effect depends on relevance, realized value, trust, suitability and reliable delivery.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Improve the quality—not only the volume—of engagement across member-only, client-only and member-client populations, allowing appropriate progression to emerge as a downstream result.

nodes.label: Products and transactions
nodes.subtitle: Banking • rewards • partner activity
nodes.definition: The banking products, reward products and transaction infrastructure through which people spend, earn and access benefits.
nodes.roleInSystem: This layer performs the institution’s core processing activity and generates signals that may indicate needs, eligibility and engagement potential.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is an established institutional capability that will be used regardless of how the future loyalty experience is designed.
nodes.known: Bank-linked products can produce additional earning routes and value. Transaction behaviour can reveal where relevant value might exist.
nodes.provisional: Product use does not itself prove loyalty or program engagement, and transaction signals cannot be treated as unrestricted targeting permission.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Reuse reliable transaction and product capabilities while connecting their outputs to permissioned decisioning and program value delivery.

nodes.label: Data and decisioning
nodes.subtitle: Priority connective layer
nodes.definition: The data, identity, analytical and decision processes used to interpret context and determine an appropriate action or opportunity.
nodes.roleInSystem: This is the most consequential connective layer identified because it links changing needs, available value, partners, products and delivery channels.
nodes.whyItMatters: The core strategic question—what value, to whom, when and through which channel—cannot be answered consistently without usable context and decision governance.
nodes.known: The client has enterprise data and offer-decisioning capabilities. Public evidence does not establish the extent to which they are integrated with the program.
nodes.provisional: More data does not guarantee better decisions. Identity gaps, consent, privacy, bias, incomplete signals and over-targeting can reduce relevance or trust.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Create permissioned, explainable decisioning that identifies where incremental value genuinely exists across members, clients and partners.

nodes.label: Channels and delivery
nodes.subtitle: Program • banking • partner touchpoints
nodes.definition: The digital, physical and communication touchpoints through which decisions, offers, information and experiences reach people.
nodes.roleInSystem: Channels translate an organizational decision into something a member or client can discover, understand and act upon.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client already operates mature banking channels, while the program also has standalone surfaces and partner touchpoints.
nodes.known: Multiple channels exist. Separate access, authentication and feature availability have produced some directional signals of discontinuity.
nodes.provisional: Multiple channels are not inherently fragmented. The quality of orchestration, ownership and handoffs across them remains unclear.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Deliver consistent context and value across the appropriate channel while preserving intentional separation where it protects privacy or accessibility.

nodes.label: Service and operations
nodes.subtitle: Fulfilment • support • recovery
nodes.definition: The operational backbone that calculates and fulfils rewards, supports members, manages issues and coordinates program administration.
nodes.roleInSystem: It converts a promised benefit into delivered value and determines what happens when that delivery fails.
nodes.whyItMatters: The financial institution already has substantial operating capacity. Reusing relevant capabilities for the program could improve consistency and create economies of scale.
nodes.known: Reliable reward posting, redemption and service recovery influence whether members trust the value proposition. Public signals identify some cross-system support handoffs.
nodes.provisional: The actual degree of integration, duplication or fragmentation between the client and program operating models is unknown.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Connect only the operational capabilities that improve fulfilment, issue ownership and cost efficiency while avoiding tightly coupled failure points.

nodes.label: Interface friction
nodes.subtitle: Partial connectivity • unclear handoffs
nodes.definition: A marker for places where identity, information, value, decisions or service may not move reliably across organizational or technological boundaries.
nodes.roleInSystem: It keeps the map attentive to the quality of interfaces without assuming that every separate system or channel is defective.
nodes.whyItMatters: Separate surfaces, linking issues, delayed rewards and support transfers provide directional evidence that some interfaces may constrain value delivery.
nodes.known: Specific member-facing breakdowns have been reported. The existence of multiple channels and systems is also supported.
nodes.provisional: Those signals do not establish enterprise-wide fragmentation or prove that tighter integration will always create net gains.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Identify which interfaces require better coordination and which separations are intentional, protective or economically sensible.

nodes.label: Permissioned identity and data
nodes.subtitle: Connected context under governance
nodes.definition: A governed ability to recognize the same person or relationship across program, banking and partner contexts where permitted.
nodes.roleInSystem: It would create the usable context required for decisioning without treating ownership as unrestricted access to all member data.
nodes.whyItMatters: Relevant orchestration depends on knowing which signals belong together and which uses the person has consented to.
nodes.known: Program and banking relationships generate different data. Privacy, consent and organizational access conditions apply to any connection.
nodes.provisional: The current identity architecture, consent model, data rights and cross-organizational access are not established.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Connect only the context required to create explainable member and partner value under clear governance.

nodes.label: Integrated value orchestration
nodes.subtitle: What value • to whom • when • where
nodes.definition: A proposed capability for selecting and coordinating the most relevant available value for a particular relationship and moment.
nodes.roleInSystem: It translates connected context into an actionable decision across program, banking and partner opportunities.
nodes.whyItMatters: The system contains many products, partners and channels. Without orchestration, additional options can increase complexity rather than realized value.
nodes.known: The client has broader offer-decisioning capabilities and has publicly emphasized personalization. Member-recognized program personalization is not yet established.
nodes.provisional: Decision relevance, operating ownership, model governance and the incremental effect on engagement remain hypotheses.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Answer the system’s core decision question consistently while respecting need, suitability, permission and channel context.

nodes.label: Coordinated delivery
nodes.subtitle: Channels • fulfilment • service recovery
nodes.definition: A future state in which relevant decisions move coherently through channels, fulfilment and service recovery.
nodes.roleInSystem: It closes the gap between selecting an opportunity and ensuring that the promised value is actually received.
nodes.whyItMatters: Relevant targeting cannot produce meaningful engagement if access, posting, redemption or issue resolution fails.
nodes.known: Channels and service capabilities already exist, while some public signals show reliability and handoff issues.
nodes.provisional: The degree of coordination required, implementation cost and risk of tightly coupled failures remain unknown.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Create fit-for-purpose continuity across discovery, action, fulfilment and recovery.

nodes.label: Broader meaningful engagement
nodes.subtitle: Across all three populations
nodes.definition: An intended increase in the quality and persistence of meaningful participation across the existing relationship base.
nodes.roleInSystem: It is the proximal future result of improving relevance, accessibility and delivery—not the final commercial outcome.
nodes.whyItMatters: Engagement applies to member-only, client-only and member-client relationships, whereas intersection growth captures only one downstream movement.
nodes.known: Research identifies observable participation behaviours and multiple engagement dimensions.
nodes.provisional: The causal effect of better data, orchestration and delivery on engagement has not yet been validated over time.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Increase engagement quality while monitoring whether it creates realized value, relationship depth and appropriate progression.

nodes.label: Larger, stronger intersection
nodes.subtitle: Appropriate movement + deeper relationships
nodes.definition: A larger and more engaged population holding both program and banking relationships.
nodes.roleInSystem: It captures the client’s desired relationship movement while distinguishing size from the quality and depth of engagement within the intersection.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client explicitly intends to convert relevant non-client members and deepen relationships with existing clients.
nodes.known: The intersection can grow through two different pathways: member-to-client conversion and client-to-member enrolment.
nodes.provisional: More linked relationships do not automatically create affinity, retention, incremental revenue or realized member value.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Grow the intersection only where the combined relationship creates demonstrable incremental value for the person and the organization.

nodes.label: Sustainable net relationship value
nodes.subtitle: Consumer + business economics
nodes.definition: The incremental economic and strategic value created across consumer and business relationships after the full cost of the program is considered.
nodes.roleInSystem: It is the client’s ultimate organizational outcome and prevents revenue growth from being assessed without the costs and liabilities required to produce it.
nodes.whyItMatters: Engagement, membership and higher spending are not sufficient evidence of ROI unless they are incremental and exceed rewards, technology, operating and risk costs.
nodes.known: Potential benefits include acquisition, product use, share of wallet, retention, partner revenue, insight and economies of scale.
nodes.provisional: Incrementality, partner economics, conversion persistence, total costs and the time required to realize returns remain unmeasured.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Build a measurement model that connects engagement and relationship movement to causal, long-term net value.

nodes.label: Non-member / non-client
nodes.subtitle: No current program or banking relationship
nodes.definition: People who are not currently loyalty-program members or banking clients of the institution.
nodes.roleInSystem: They sit outside the active relationship system because the current inquiry focuses on engagement and movement among people who already hold at least one relationship.
nodes.whyItMatters: Their eventual entry matters for growth, but modelling acquisition tactics in detail would expand the inquiry beyond the activation and relationship system currently being examined.
nodes.known: A person could enter the boundary by joining the program, becoming a banking client, or establishing both relationships.
nodes.provisional: The size, needs, awareness and likelihood of entry for this population have not been established by the current research.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Treat boundary entry as a downstream consequence of the system’s reputation and value—not as the primary behaviour the present map must explain.

systemLinks.explanation: These are the two primary entry states if a person establishes one relationship.
These outcomes may strengthen reputation and create entry reasons, but the connection remains indirect and is not drawn as an internal flow.

nodes.label: Customer expectations and market norms
nodes.subtitle: Personalization • simplicity • flexibility • trust
nodes.definition: Changing expectations about relevance, personalization, ease of use, flexibility, transparency and dependable service.
nodes.roleInSystem: This influence shapes the standard against which people judge program, banking and partner value without being controlled by the bounded system.
nodes.whyItMatters: The client’s problem statement explicitly links the need for deeper relationships to changing customer needs, while primary research emphasizes flexibility, relevance and reliable value delivery.
nodes.known: Members compare loyalty value against alternative programs, cash equivalents, service expectations and the effort required to use benefits.
nodes.provisional: The relative importance of each expectation varies by population, context and moment; the map does not assume one universal preference profile.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Use expectations as a design and validation condition rather than treating personalization or engagement as inherently valuable.

systemLinks.explanation: Expectations shape whether available value feels understandable, accessible and worth continued participation.
Future capabilities would need to meet evolving expectations without over-personalizing or increasing complexity.

nodes.label: Technology landscape
nodes.subtitle: AI • identity • open-data capabilities
nodes.definition: The changing availability and maturity of technologies that can support prediction, personalization, identity resolution, data portability and coordinated delivery.
nodes.roleInSystem: It changes what may be technically possible, expected or economically feasible, but it does not determine which capabilities should be adopted.
nodes.whyItMatters: Artificial intelligence and data portability may expand decisioning options while also creating new governance, trust and operating requirements.
nodes.known: The institution has broader enterprise data and AI ambitions. Program-specific integration and demonstrated member value remain unconfirmed.
nodes.provisional: Technology maturity, implementation cost, model quality, interoperability and incremental impact on engagement are unresolved.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Evaluate technology only where it improves a defined value or operating flow under appropriate governance.

systemLinks.explanation: External technology options may improve or complicate how signals, decisions and fulfilment move across existing capabilities.
These hypothesized capabilities depend partly on available technology, but technology alone does not establish their value or feasibility.

nodes.label: Regulation, privacy and consent environment
nodes.subtitle: Permitted use • accountability • protection
nodes.definition: The laws, regulatory expectations, privacy rules and consent conditions governing the collection, connection, use and exchange of data and value.
nodes.roleInSystem: This environment defines permissible operating conditions for identity, decisioning, marketing, partner insight and cross-system data use.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ownership of a program does not imply unrestricted access to or use of member information; permission and purpose remain necessary conditions.
nodes.known: Privacy, consent, suitability and governance requirements apply to any connection between program, banking and partner contexts.
nodes.provisional: The specific legal interpretation, data rights, consent architecture and partner-sharing limits are outside the present research scope.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Treat governance as a design input from the outset rather than a downstream compliance check.

systemLinks.explanation: Regulatory and consent conditions affect which signals may be used, which actions are suitable and what information may flow to partners.
Governance defines the operating envelope for the future pathway and may intentionally preserve separation between some systems.

nodes.label: Competitor loyalty and financial ecosystems
nodes.subtitle: Alternative programs • products • value propositions
nodes.definition: Other loyalty, banking, card and partner ecosystems against which people and businesses compare the client’s value proposition.
nodes.roleInSystem: Competitors provide alternative relationships, benefits and participation options without being actors inside the bounded client-program system.
nodes.whyItMatters: Primary research shows that members compare reward economics, flexibility, perks and service across multiple programs rather than evaluating one program in isolation.
nodes.known: Alternative reward products and ecosystems affect members’ reference points and can compete for spending, attention and partner participation.
nodes.provisional: Competitor-specific performance, switching behaviour and direct effects on this program have not been measured in the current analysis.
nodes.opportunityImplication: Use competitor ecosystems as contextual benchmarks while preserving a member-value definition grounded in actual needs rather than feature imitation.

systemLinks.explanation: Alternative programs affect value comparisons, participation choices and the attractiveness of the partner network.
Competitive responses may influence whether improved engagement persists and produces incremental organizational value.

relationships.label: Member signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Program activity can reveal preferences, value-seeking behaviour and potential needs where use is permitted.

relationships.label: Client signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Banking and broader rewards behaviour may indicate where program participation could create incremental value.

relationships.label: Combined signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: The intersection may provide richer context, but only when identity, consent and permitted use are resolved.

relationships.label: Partner signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Offer, transaction and fulfilment information helps evaluate partner relevance and performance.

relationships.label: Permissioned context
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Existing signals become usable decision inputs only after governance, identity and consent conditions are met.

relationships.label: Relevant decision
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Decisioning selects an appropriate opportunity, audience, moment and delivery route.

relationships.label: Delivered value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: A decision becomes meaningful only when the opportunity is understood, accessible and fulfilled.

relationships.label: Appropriate progression
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Repeated relevant engagement may support conversion or relationship depth, but the effect is not automatic.

relationships.label: Relationship economics
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Relationship movement must create incremental value after costs rather than simply more linked accounts.

relationships.label: Consumer + business value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Partners may create consumer revenue, partner economics and deeper business relationships simultaneously.

relationships.label: Banking adoption
relationships.relationshipDefinition: A member-only participant enters the intersection when a relevant banking need leads to product adoption.

relationships.label: Program enrolment
relationships.relationshipDefinition: A client-only participant enters the intersection by joining and beginning to use the program.

relationships.label: Open program participation
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Members can earn, redeem and use partner value without becoming banking clients.

relationships.label: Combined participation
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Member-clients can access program value alongside eligible bank-connected benefits.

relationships.label: Offers + experiences
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Partner contributions expand the ways members can earn, save, access or realize value.

relationships.label: Purchases + preference
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Member activity returns sales, attention, affinity and potential share-of-wallet value to partners.

relationships.label: Realized value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Value must move beyond availability into an outcome the person can recognize and use.

relationships.label: Transaction signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Product activity supplies behavioural context to the data and decisioning layer.

relationships.label: Decisions + opportunities
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Decisioning outputs must move into a channel before a person can discover or act on them.

relationships.label: Opportunity delivery
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Channels translate selected value into a visible and actionable member experience.

relationships.label: Fulfilment + recovery
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Operations deliver the promise and determine how failures are corrected.

relationships.label: Outcome signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Participation and outcomes create feedback for measurement and future decisions.

relationships.label: Identity + data handoffs
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Separate identities or permissions may interrupt the movement of usable context.

relationships.label: Channel continuity
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Separate surfaces may create repeated steps, inconsistent context or unclear ownership.

relationships.label: Support ownership
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Cross-system issues may be transferred between teams rather than resolved end to end.

relationships.label: Unified permissioned context
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Governed identity and data create the context required for more relevant orchestration.

relationships.label: Coordinated decisions
relationships.relationshipDefinition: The chosen action is carried consistently into delivery, fulfilment and service processes.

relationships.label: Reliable relevant value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Future coordination aims to make relevant value easier to access and dependable to receive.

relationships.label: Partner matching + insight
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Partners can be matched to relevant needs and receive useful performance feedback in return.

relationships.label: Realized value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Value must move beyond availability into an outcome the person can recognize and use.

relationships.label: Appropriate progression
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Repeated relevant engagement may support conversion or relationship depth, but the effect is not automatic.

relationships.label: Relationship economics
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Relationship movement must create incremental value after costs rather than simply more linked accounts.

relationships.label: Consumer + business value
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Partners may create consumer revenue, partner economics and deeper business relationships simultaneously.

relationships.label: Governance context
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Regulation, privacy and consent conditions shape which emerging technologies and uses are permissible.

relationships.label: Capability signals
relationships.relationshipDefinition: New technological possibilities can raise expectations for relevance, immediacy, portability and ease of use.

relationships.label: Market reference points
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Competing ecosystems influence the standards people use to compare value, flexibility, service and access.

relationships.label: Alternative value propositions
relationships.relationshipDefinition: People outside the boundary can choose alternative loyalty and financial relationships before entering this system.

relationships.label: Entry expectations
relationships.relationshipDefinition: Expectations about value, trust and effort shape the threshold for establishing a first relationship.
